text.overview: The Hawk Hover Tank represents the modern commercial revival of an ancient light combat vehicle originally fielded by the Terran Hegemony in 2464 under the designation LTV-4. General Mechanics of Mars developed the original design as a fast, affordable platform licensed broadly to Star League member states across the Inner Sphere. After the Succession Wars erased most of that production network, Quikscell Company reintroduced the design in the early thirty-first century under the Hawk designation. Quikscell markets the Hawk as a companion to the faster Falcon, offering buyers a slower but harder-hitting variant optimized for long-range direct fire rather than the close-range tactics favored by its sibling. The vehicle appeals to militia commanders and peripheral governments seeking affordable long-range fire support without the cost of fusion-powered combat vehicles.
text.capabilities:
The Hawk's primary armament is a particle cannon that provides reliable long-range direct fire well suited to engaging lightly armored vehicles and suppressing infantry at standoff range. A single short-range missile rack supplements this main weapon with close-quarters capability when engagements close to shorter distances, though the limited ammunition supply encourages conservative fire discipline during extended engagements. Hover propulsion enables the Hawk to cross water obstacles, swamps, and broken terrain that would stop tracked or wheeled vehicles, allowing it to reposition across ground that heavier pursuers cannot follow. This combination of long-range firepower and terrain-crossing mobility suits the Hawk to screening, harassment, and fire support missions rather than direct assault roles where sustained exposure to return fire would be fatal.

ProtecTech Light armor provides baseline crew protection against small arms and glancing fire but cannot absorb concentrated weapons fire from combat vehicles or BattleMechs. Basix 200 communications and OptiSight-12 targeting equipment handle fire control and coordination adequately for the vehicle's intended mission profile. The ICE powerplant keeps fuel and maintenance requirements within reach of backwater logistics infrastructure, a practical advantage for the peripheral militias forming the Hawk's primary market, though it constrains operational range when the vehicle operates far from established resupply points.
text.deployment: The Hawk appears in militia and mercenary inventories throughout the Inner Sphere, typically fielded in screening, long-range harassment, and fire support roles. Its particle cannon allows engagement at distances beyond the reach of most light vehicle adversaries, while hover mobility enables positioning on flanks and across terrain that challenges wheeled and tracked pursuit. Commanders pair the Hawk with Falcons when available, using its range to suppress enemy formations while faster vehicles maneuver for close-range attacks. Peripheral militias favor it as the most affordable long-range fire option available through Quikscell's distribution network.
text.battleHistory:
General Mechanics produced the LTV-4 on Mars for the Terran Hegemony, and licensed production spread the design across Star League member states during the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth centuries. Amaris Armored Vehicles assembled it on Erdvynn and Timbuktu during the Rim Worlds Republic's later years, though both facilities were presumably destroyed during the Amaris Coup. Buda Imperial Vehicles produced the type for the Draconis Combine from Dabih until that factory's destruction in 2883. Veridian Dynamics operated a Federated Suns production line on Torrence until 2989, and Cyclops Incorporated maintained a licensed Lyran line on Skye that collapsed during the Succession Wars. Exeter Organization retooled its Keystone plant to manufacture the Pegasus Hovertank in 2791 rather than continue LTV-4 output. Brooks Incorporated assembled units at Suzano under Capellan license during the Star League era, though that facility was destroyed before 3000. The LTV-4 designation itself gradually faded from common usage as the production network dissolved.

Quikscell Company revived the design in the early 3020s, rebranding it the Hawk to complement the Falcon they had just introduced. The company sold the Hawk through the same partially assembled kit system applied across all Quikscell products, packaging the vehicle in crates of components with assembly instructions. Buyers on frontier worlds frequently lacked the technical staff to assemble the kits without assistance, requiring contracted mercenary technicians to complete installation. This persistent complaint failed to dent the Hawk's commercial appeal, as its low acquisition price remained difficult to match among comparable long-range combat vehicles.
text.notes: Experimental until 2470. Originally known as the LTV-4 Hover Tank in XTR: Primitives Vol 2.

text.deployment: The first Hawk Moth production run shipped in its entirety to the Free Worlds League per the Imperator contract, distributed to multiple regiments of the Free Worlds Legionnaires. Subsequent production reached buyers across the Inner Sphere. The Hawk Moth became a standard element of cavalry and harassment formations, valued for its ability to range ahead of ground columns and attrit targets from beyond effective response distance. Production continued at Ruchbah through the Jihad and Republic eras under successive owners of the facility, with Kallon Weapon Industries on Loyalty adding production capacity during the Republic period.

A custom refit of the standard Hawk Moth with unknown origin, this variant is reconfigured for close-range and anti-personnel work rather than the standoff sniping that defines the base design. The standard long-range armament is removed and replaced by a Rotary AC/5 and Machine Gun in a VTOL chin turret, providing a full 360-degree firing arc effective against both armored vehicles and unarmored infantry. A fuel cell engine replaces the standard powerplant, freeing enough mass for two tons of heavy ferro-fibrous armor that provide substantially more protection than the base model. The reduced weapon range is an intentional trade-off suited to this variant's apparent close-support role.

This variant trades one ton of ammunition for an additional ton of armor, nearly doubling the base model's protection. The trade-off shortens the useful engagement window before resupply is needed, but appeals to commanders who expect their VTOLs to operate in contested airspace where interception attempts are likely. The Armor variant served alongside the base model across the Inner Sphere in cavalry and fire support roles throughout the Clan Invasion era and beyond.

Emerging from Ruchbah's Michaelson facilities under Word of Blake occupation, the Thunderbolt variant replaces the standard armament with a Doombud Thunderbolt 15 launcher, trading extreme range for decisive burst damage. The internal combustion engine is replaced by a fuel cell, freeing mass for improved armor while maintaining speed. A Mast Mount fitted to the rotor head allows the vehicle to hold hull-down firing positions, engaging targets while maximizing cover. The variant appeared in combat on multiple worlds during the Jihad, and Kallon Weapon Industries on Loyalty continued its production following the conflict.

Introduced in 3114, this variant drops both SRM launchers in favor of a pair of five-tubed Multi-Missile Launchers with two tons of ammunition. The ability to switch between short and long-range missiles in a single launcher gives this variant greater tactical flexibility than the base model, particularly useful when engagement distances vary during raids or pursuit operations. It served alongside the standard variant in Republic and Lyran formations throughout the Dark Age.

This variant replaces the standard armament with a single Class 2 Hyper-Velocity Autocannon carrying 30 rounds, paired with a VTOL jet booster capable of briefly pushing the craft to over 220 km/h for rapid repositioning or disengagement. Despite its theoretical utility, the variant is broadly considered unpopular among pilots. The HV autocannon's high visual signature undermines the vehicle's ability to approach undetected, and the light damage output makes the trade-off difficult to justify outside dedicated overwatch roles.

text.overview: The Heavy BattleMech Recovery Vehicle is a less common but strategically important companion to the standard recovery vehicle, found primarily in the support echelons of heavy and assault BattleMech formations. Where the standard recovery vehicle is limited in what it can haul, the heavy version is capable of loading and transporting any BattleMech currently in production across the Inner Sphere, making it an irreplaceable asset when an assault machine goes down in recoverable condition. Like its lighter counterpart, it is produced across numerous facilities without a single dominant manufacturer, ensuring availability wherever heavy BattleMech forces are deployed.
text.capabilities: The Heavy BattleMech Recovery Vehicle is considerably larger and more capable than the standard model, rated to load and haul payloads up to one hundred tons. This capacity allows it to recover any BattleMech currently produced, including the heaviest assault designs. A Generic 260 ICE power plant moves the seventy-ton vehicle at a cruising speed of 43 kilometers per hour unloaded, but this figure drops sharply in practice. When loaded with any BattleMech weighing more than thirty tons, the heavy recovery vehicle slows to approximately 32 kilometers per hour, a pace that leaves recovery crews dangerously exposed in contested territory. To partially offset this vulnerability, the vehicle carries significantly more armor than the standard recovery version, protecting the crew during the unavoidably slow extraction process. No weapons or targeting systems are fitted, and communications equipment is sourced from whatever is locally available.
text.deployment: The Heavy BattleMech Recovery Vehicle is concentrated in the support echelons of heavy and assault BattleMech formations, where its rated payload capacity justifies the additional logistical burden. Units supporting assault lances typically maintain at least one HBMRV, while lighter forces may share access to heavy recovery assets at the regimental or brigade level. Despite its slow pace under load, the HBMRV's ability to recover any BattleMech currently in service makes it irreplaceable when an assault machine goes down in recoverable condition. Crews are trained to minimize exposure time during recovery, selecting concealed routes and requesting fire support coverage whenever the tactical situation allows.
text.battleHistory:
The Heavy BattleMech Recovery Vehicle entered service alongside the growing prevalence of assault-weight BattleMechs, whose mass exceeded the rated recovery capacity of standard vehicles. Early Star League-era commanders quickly recognized that losing an assault machine to an irrecoverable breakdown was an unacceptable outcome, and dedicated heavy recovery platforms were developed to address the gap. Like the standard BMRV, the heavy variant was never tied to a single manufacturer, relying instead on generic component specifications that could be sourced and assembled at facilities across the Inner Sphere.

The Succession Wars placed additional stress on heavy recovery assets, as the losses sustained in major engagements meant that assault-weight machines became increasingly precious. Units operating assault lances often prioritized maintaining at least one heavy recovery vehicle, even at the cost of other support assets. The increased armor protection compared to the standard BMRV reflects lessons learned during this period, as recovery vehicles operating in partially-secured zones found that the extra mass of an assault mech load extended their exposure time dangerously.

text.capabilities:
The Heavy Hover APC carries six tons of infantry -- sufficient for two full platoons of standard foot infantry or one platoon of motorized or jump troops -- making it the largest hover-mobile personnel carrier in common service. An internal combustion engine propels the twenty-ton vehicle to a maximum speed of approximately one hundred thirty kilometers per hour, fast enough for rapid insertions though especially slower than the ten-ton standard hover APC. Two front-mounted machine guns provide anti-infantry defense during approach and withdrawal.

Fifty-six points of standard armor provide substantially better protection than the standard APC, though the design concentrates armor heavily on the front and flanks at the expense of the rear, which houses the assault ramp for troop deployment. The lack of a turret limits the machine guns to a forward-only firing arc, leaving the vehicle vulnerable to flanking attacks. This trade-off reflects the design philosophy of a vehicle that approaches the enemy head-on, deploys its infantry, and withdraws before lateral threats can develop.
text.deployment: The Heavy Hover APC serves with mobile forces across the Inner Sphere, particularly those formations requiring rapid deployment of infantry in strength. The Federated Commonwealth's Regimental Combat Teams fielded large numbers, using the hover variant's speed to rapidly insert two-platoon infantry formations in support of BattleMech advances. Post-Jihad successor states maintain the design in similar roles, valuing its ability to deliver meaningful infantry strength at hover speeds.

text.capabilities:
The LRM variant of the Heavy Hover APC supplements the standard front-mounted machine guns with an LRM-5 launcher while reducing infantry carrying capacity from six tons to three tons -- enough for one platoon of standard infantry. This trade-off provides organic long-range fire support for the infantry being delivered, allowing the vehicle to soften targets during its approach run. Two machine guns and one ton of LRM ammunition complement the missile launcher.

Fifty-six points of standard armor and a maximum speed of approximately one hundred thirty kilometers per hour give the LRM variant the same protection and mobility as the base model. The halved troop capacity means commanders must weigh the benefit of integral fire support against the reduced infantry strength delivered per vehicle, typically deploying LRM variants alongside standard models in mixed formations.
text.deployment: The LRM variant serves in mixed formations alongside standard Heavy Hover APCs, providing organic fire support during high-speed insertion operations. Commands deploying the Heavy Hover APC in offensive roles typically assign one LRM variant per lance of standard transports, balancing fire support against total infantry delivery capacity.

text.capabilities:
The machine gun variant of the Heavy Hover APC replaces half the infantry carrying capacity with additional machine guns positioned to provide all-around anti-infantry coverage. Carrying three tons of infantry -- one platoon -- the vehicle mounts two front-facing machine guns, one on each flank, and two rear-facing machine guns, ensuring no approach is undefended. A full ton and a half of ammunition sustains the six-gun battery through extended engagements.

This configuration excels as an escort vehicle in convoy operations, where its all-around machine gun coverage can suppress ambush forces from any direction while still delivering a platoon of infantry to reinforce threatened positions. The same fifty-six points of armor and approximately one hundred thirty kilometers per hour maximum speed as the base model ensure the MG variant can keep pace with the formation it protects.
text.deployment: The MG variant serves primarily as a convoy escort and perimeter security vehicle, where its all-around machine gun coverage protects slower vehicles and deployed infantry positions. The hover chassis's speed allows it to rapidly respond to threats along the length of a convoy column, making it particularly valuable in hostile territory where ambushes are expected.

text.capabilities:
The Scout Tank variant of the Heavy Hover APC entirely removes the infantry compartment and converts the chassis into a dedicated reconnaissance vehicle. A front-mounted Light Autocannon/5 with two tons of ammunition provides the primary armament, offering accurate fire against light vehicles and soft targets at medium range. The complete elimination of troop-carrying capacity reflects this variant's purely combat-oriented role.

Ferro-fibrous armor provides sixty-two points of protection -- more than any other Heavy Hover APC variant -- while CASE protects the crew from ammunition explosions. The combination of enhanced armor, a medium-range weapon, and the hover chassis's approximately one hundred thirty kilometer per hour speed creates an effective light reconnaissance platform. Originally developed during the Jihad era, the Scout Tank demonstrates how the Heavy APC chassis can be adapted well beyond its original transport mission.
text.deployment: The Scout Tank variant serves exclusively in reconnaissance formations, having entirely abandoned the transport role in favor of dedicated scouting capability. Introduced during the Jihad era, this conversion found adoption with forces requiring a light, fast reconnaissance platform that could be produced using the well-established Heavy Hover APC manufacturing base rather than purpose-built scout vehicle production lines.

text.capabilities:
The SRM variant of the Heavy Hover APC adds an SRM-4 launcher to the front-mounted machine gun battery while reducing infantry carrying capacity from six tons to three tons -- enough for one platoon of standard infantry. The SRM-4 provides meaningful close-range anti-armor capability, allowing the vehicle to engage light armored targets and support its delivered infantry against vehicular threats. Two machine guns and one ton of SRM ammunition complement the launcher.

Fifty-six points of standard armor and a maximum speed of approximately one hundred thirty kilometers per hour maintain the base model's survivability profile. The SRM variant fills a light cavalry role, using hover speed to dash forward, deliver infantry, and provide short-range fire support before withdrawing, with the SRM-4 giving it substantially more punch against armored targets than the machine-gun-only base model.
text.deployment: The SRM variant fills a light cavalry role, using hover speed to deliver infantry and provide close-range fire support against armored threats. Commands operating in environments where light vehicles and combat hovercraft pose significant threats favor this variant, as the SRM-4 provides a meaningful deterrent that the base model's machine guns cannot match.

text.capabilities:
The EN Variant replaces the standard Delta Dart launchers with a mixed battery of two Enhanced LRM-15 and two Extended LRM-15 launchers, providing complementary engagement ranges. A 160-rated extralight fusion engine maintains the same thirty-two kilometer per hour top speed while freeing tonnage for hardened armor plating that provides exceptional resistance to ballistic weapons.

The hardened armor makes the EN Variant substantially more survivable than the original Heavy LRM Carrier, capable of withstanding heavy PPC strikes on any facing. The experimental nature of the enhanced and extended-range missiles results in reduced ammunition capacity compared to standard launchers, and the prototype status limits production volume.
text.deployment: The EN Variant was produced at Johnston Industries' Mobile Fabrication Facility A on Lackland beginning in 3073. Just under two lances of completed vehicles were shipped to the Pleiades worlds for extensive field testing during the Jihad. The experimental production facility's unpredictable output rate limited deployment numbers.

text.overview: The Heavy MML Carrier is an eighty-ton tracked combat vehicle developed by Majesty Metals and Manufacturing as a Jihad-era evolution of the Heavy LRM Carrier. Replacing the four dedicated LRM launchers with six versatile MML-9 launchers, the design trades raw long-range firepower for tactical flexibility, capable of engaging targets at both long and short range without changing ammunition types. The vehicle retains the Heavy LRM Carrier's turret configuration and basic chassis.

The Heavy NLRM Carrier is an eighty-ton tracked combat vehicle developed by Johnston Industries and Joint Equipment Systems as an advanced fire support platform for the Federated Suns. Introduced in 3083, the design adapts the Heavy LRM Carrier chassis with next-generation enhanced long-range missiles, hardened armor, and a fuel cell engine, producing a substantially more survivable and technologically sophisticated vehicle than its Periphery-origin predecessor.

text.capabilities:
The Heavy Tracked APC carries six tons of infantry -- sufficient for two full platoons of standard foot infantry or one platoon of motorized or jump troops -- on a robust tracked chassis that can negotiate virtually any terrain. An internal combustion engine propels the twenty-ton vehicle to a maximum speed of approximately eighty-six kilometers per hour, making it the slowest of the three Heavy APC configurations but the most reliable in rough terrain. Two front-mounted machine guns provide anti-infantry defense.

Fifty-six points of standard armor provide the same level of protection as the hover and wheeled heavy variants, concentrated on the front and flanks with reduced rear coverage around the assault ramp. The tracked drive system's all-terrain capability makes this variant the preferred transport for operations in rough, forested, or mountainous terrain where hover vehicles cannot operate and wheeled vehicles struggle. The lack of a turret restricts machine gun fire to the forward arc.
text.deployment: The Heavy Tracked APC is the preferred heavy transport for formations operating in rough terrain, where its tracked drive system provides reliable mobility that hover and wheeled vehicles cannot match. The Draconis Combine and Free Worlds League field particularly large numbers, favoring the tracked variant's all-terrain capability for operations across their varied and often undeveloped frontier worlds.

text.capabilities:
The LRM variant of the Heavy Tracked APC adds a front-mounted LRM-5 launcher alongside the standard machine gun pair while reducing infantry carrying capacity from six tons to three tons -- enough for one platoon of standard infantry. This conversion provides organic indirect fire support for the transported troops, with one ton of LRM ammunition sustaining fire through a typical engagement. The tracked chassis allows the LRM variant to reach hull-down firing positions in rough terrain inaccessible to wheeled or hover vehicles.

With fifty-six points of standard armor and a maximum speed of approximately eighty-six kilometers per hour, the tracked LRM variant trades mobility for tactical flexibility, capable of providing fire support from covered positions while still delivering infantry to the objective. The tracked drive system's reliability in poor conditions makes this variant particularly valuable in defensive operations where terrain advantage offsets the slower approach speed.
text.deployment: The tracked LRM variant serves alongside standard Heavy Tracked APCs in combined-arms formations, providing fire support from positions in rough terrain. The tracked chassis's ability to reach concealed firing positions in mountains and forests gives commanders flexible deployment options unavailable to hover or wheeled LRM variants.

text.capabilities:
The machine gun variant of the Heavy Tracked APC replaces half the infantry carrying capacity with additional machine guns positioned for all-around coverage. Carrying three tons of infantry -- one platoon -- the vehicle mounts two front-facing machine guns, one on each flank, and two rear-facing machine guns, ensuring comprehensive anti-infantry protection from every direction. A full ton and a half of ammunition sustains the six-gun battery through extended operations.

The tracked MG variant excels in urban warfare and jungle operations where ambushes can come from any direction and the tracked drive system provides reliable mobility through rubble-strewn streets and dense undergrowth. Fifty-six points of standard armor and all-around machine gun coverage make it an effective convoy escort in hostile territory, capable of suppressing infantry threats while still delivering a platoon to reinforce critical positions.
text.deployment: The tracked MG variant excels in urban warfare and jungle operations, where all-around machine gun coverage is essential and the tracked drive system's ability to navigate rubble and dense vegetation provides a critical mobility advantage. Garrison forces defending cities and industrial complexes frequently deploy this variant as a mobile strongpoint.

text.capabilities:
The SRM variant of the Heavy Tracked APC adds a front-mounted SRM-4 launcher to the standard machine gun pair while reducing infantry carrying capacity from six tons to three tons -- enough for one platoon of standard infantry. The SRM-4 provides meaningful anti-armor capability at close range, allowing the vehicle to engage light combat vehicles and threaten BattleMech rear armor while fulfilling its transport mission. Two machine guns and one ton of SRM ammunition complement the launcher.

Fifty-six points of standard armor and the tracked drive system's all-terrain capability make this the most tactically versatile Heavy APC variant, able to deliver infantry and provide close fire support across any terrain type. The slower maximum speed of approximately eighty-six kilometers per hour is offset by the tracked chassis's ability to approach through terrain that faster hover and wheeled vehicles must avoid.
text.deployment: The tracked SRM variant fills a combined transport and escort role, delivering infantry while providing close-range fire support against armored threats encountered during approach. The tracked chassis's ability to follow dismounted infantry across rough terrain makes it valuable as a persistent fire support element that can remain with its delivered troops.

text.overview: The Heavy Transport B1 is the militarized variant of a broad family of wheeled freight vehicles that have supported both civilian and military logistics networks since their introduction in 2370. Ranging from cargo vans to full tractor-trailer configurations, heavy transports fill the unglamorous but essential role of moving supplies, ammunition, and equipment wherever dedicated military transport assets are unavailable or impractical. The B1 designation marks the armed version of this family, fitted with minimal self-defense weaponry while retaining the design's core cargo capacity. Its combination of reasonable on-road speed and low acquisition cost has made it a common sight across the Inner Sphere, valued more for reliability than for any tactical distinction.
text.capabilities:
The Heavy Transport B1 prioritizes cargo capacity and road mobility over fighting ability. Powered by a five-ton internal combustion engine, the vehicle reaches a top on-road speed approaching 85 km/h, allowing it to keep pace with most mechanized supply columns. The vehicle's primary payload is a seven-ton cargo bay, sufficient for ammunition loads, equipment crates, or general military supplies. Three tons of armor provide modest protection against small arms fire and light infantry weapons, enough to discourage opportunistic ambushes but wholly insufficient against any serious military engagement.

The standard armament is a single SRM-2 with one ton of reloads. Depending on the variant, this weapon is either forward-mounted and fired by the driver or atop the vehicle on a turret operated by a dedicated gunner. The B1 is not designed to fight its way out of trouble. Its greatest strengths are its low acquisition cost, ease of maintenance, and the wide availability of replacement parts across virtually every inhabited world in the Inner Sphere. These qualities come at the price of near-zero survivability once a vehicle enters a contested engagement.
text.deployment: The standard B1 serves in rear-area logistics and supply roles across virtually every faction in the Inner Sphere. Its SRM-2 provides token defense against infantry ambushes and light vehicle threats encountered along contested supply routes. Commanders typically deploy these vehicles in small convoys with some form of armed escort when operating near active front lines, relying on numbers and speed rather than firepower to ensure cargo reaches its destination.
text.battleHistory:
Heavy transports have been a fixture of military logistics since the earliest days of interstellar warfare. The B1 variant emerged in 2370 as the standard armed configuration within a family of generic wheeled freight vehicles, filling the practical need for cargo-carrying platforms capable of operating in contested rear areas without requiring dedicated escort at all times.

The design's simplicity and lack of proprietary components allowed it to be produced and maintained by a wide range of manufacturers across multiple factions throughout the centuries. This distributed production model proved especially valuable during the Succession Wars, when the disruption of interstellar supply chains left armies dependent on whatever could be fabricated or repaired locally. The B1's basic construction and interchangeable weapon mounts made it a natural fit for that environment, outlasting many more sophisticated designs simply because it could be kept running with locally available materials and minimal technical expertise.

Neither glamorous nor tactically impressive, the Heavy Transport B1 represents the kind of mundane engineering that keeps armies fed, armed, and functional. Its continued presence across virtually every era of BattleTech history reflects a simple truth: whatever the political situation, someone always needs to move cargo from one place to another.

text.overview: The Heavy Weapons Carrier is a twenty-ton hover vehicle mounting a single turret-mounted PPC. Associated with the Gray Death Legion's operations on Glengarry, this fast reconnaissance and harassment platform trades the weapons carrier family's traditional tracked chassis for a hovercraft capable of one hundred thirty kilometers per hour. The fusion engine provides unlimited range, making it well-suited for extended patrol and raiding operations.
text.capabilities:
The Heavy Weapons Carrier mounts a single turret-mounted PPC as its sole armament, providing significant firepower for a twenty-ton platform. A fusion engine drives the hover chassis to one hundred thirty kilometers per hour, making it one of the fastest combat vehicles in service. The turret mount allows engagement in any direction without repositioning.

Three tons of standard armor provide minimal protection, making the vehicle extremely vulnerable to return fire. The design relies entirely on its exceptional speed and the PPC's long range to avoid sustained engagement. The fusion engine provides unlimited operational range, well-suited for the extended patrol and harassment missions the vehicle is designed to perform.
text.deployment: The Heavy Weapons Carrier is associated with the Gray Death Legion's operations on Glengarry in 3056. The vehicle's exceptional speed and PPC armament made it effective for reconnaissance-in-force and harassment missions against Clan Jade Falcon forces. No large-scale production or widespread adoption has been documented.
text.battleHistory:
The Heavy Weapons Carrier appeared in the Historical Turning Points: Glengarry scenario pack, associated with the Gray Death Legion's defense of Glengarry in 3056. The vehicle's design reflects the Legion's preference for fast, hard-hitting platforms capable of hit-and-run tactics against heavier forces. No manufacturer data is available, suggesting the vehicle may be a field modification or limited-production design rather than a mass-manufactured platform.

Sarna notes the vehicle is one ton underweight, suggesting a possible errata issue in the original publication. Despite this discrepancy, the design serves as an example of the diverse light combat vehicles fielded by mercenary commands during the Clan Invasion era.

production.manufacturer: Quikscell Company|Amaris Armored Vehicles|Gienah Combat Vehicles|Quikscell Company|Buda Imperial Vehicles|Maxwell Planetary Defense Consortium|General Motors|Hellespont Industrials|Taurus Territorial Industries|Aldis Industries

text.capabilities:
The Heavy Wheeled APC carries six tons of infantry -- sufficient for two full platoons of standard foot infantry or one platoon of motorized or jump troops -- on a twenty-ton wheeled chassis optimized for operations on improved surfaces. An internal combustion engine provides a maximum speed of approximately ninety-seven kilometers per hour, making this the fastest of the three Heavy APC configurations on roads and paved surfaces. Two front-mounted machine guns provide anti-infantry defense.

Fifty-six points of standard armor provide the same protection as the hover and tracked heavy variants, with the same front-heavy distribution and reduced rear coverage around the assault ramp. The wheeled drive system excels in urban and garrison environments where established road networks enable rapid transit between positions, though it struggles in rough terrain compared to the tracked variant. The lack of a turret restricts machine gun fire to the forward arc.
text.deployment: The Heavy Wheeled APC serves primarily in garrison and urban defense formations, where established road networks support its wheeled drive system and the environment suits its forward-oriented weapons layout. The Lyran Commonwealth fields large numbers for operations along its extensive road networks, while planetary defense forces across the Inner Sphere favor the design for garrison duties in developed areas.

text.capabilities:
The LRM variant of the Heavy Wheeled APC supplements the front-mounted machine guns with an LRM-5 launcher while reducing infantry carrying capacity from six tons to three tons -- enough for one platoon of standard infantry. One ton of LRM ammunition provides adequate endurance for typical engagements. The wheeled chassis's road speed allows the LRM variant to rapidly reposition between firing positions using established road networks.

Fifty-six points of standard armor and a maximum speed of approximately ninety-seven kilometers per hour maintain the base model's survivability and mobility. Garrison forces defending urban areas and industrial complexes favor this variant, as the road network dependence is less of a limitation in developed environments and the LRM-5 provides useful standoff capability for defensive operations.
text.deployment: The wheeled LRM variant serves garrison forces in developed environments, where road networks support rapid repositioning between firing positions. This variant sees particular use in defensive operations around cities and industrial complexes, where the LRM-5 provides useful standoff capability against approaching forces.

text.capabilities:
The machine gun variant of the Heavy Wheeled APC replaces half the infantry carrying capacity with additional machine guns for all-around coverage. Carrying three tons of infantry -- one platoon -- the vehicle mounts two front-facing machine guns, one on each flank, and two rear-facing machine guns, providing comprehensive anti-personnel protection from every direction. A full ton and a half of ammunition sustains the six-gun battery through extended operations.

The wheeled MG variant excels in urban patrol and convoy escort duties, where its all-around machine gun coverage and road-optimized speed allow it to respond rapidly to threats from any direction. Fifty-six points of standard armor and approximately ninety-seven kilometers per hour on improved surfaces make it the fastest MG-equipped Heavy APC, well-suited to the rapid-response role in garrison and security operations.
text.deployment: The wheeled MG variant serves security and garrison forces in urban environments, providing all-around anti-infantry coverage at road speeds. Its six machine guns and heavy armor make it the most firepower-dense patrol vehicle available in the Heavy APC family, and many urban defense commands use it as their primary security vehicle.

text.capabilities:
The SRM variant of the Heavy Wheeled APC adds a front-mounted SRM-4 launcher to the standard machine gun pair while reducing infantry carrying capacity from six tons to three tons -- enough for one platoon of standard infantry. The SRM-4 provides anti-armor capability at close range, with two machine guns and one ton of SRM ammunition complementing the launcher. This conversion gives the wheeled transport meaningful offensive capability against light armored targets.

Fifty-six points of standard armor and a maximum speed of approximately ninety-seven kilometers per hour maintain the base model's protection and road mobility. The wheeled SRM variant is most effective in developed environments where road networks support rapid approach to engagement range, deploying its infantry and providing SRM fire support before withdrawing along the same routes.
text.deployment: The wheeled SRM variant serves garrison and urban defense forces, providing anti-armor fire support alongside troop delivery in developed environments. The combination of SRM-4 capability and road-optimized speed makes it effective for rapid-reaction forces responding to armored incursions in urban areas.

text.capabilities:
The Word of Blake variant of the Heavy Wheeled APC stands as a radical upgrade to the standard design, replacing the internal combustion engine with an extralight fusion engine that boosts maximum speed to approximately one hundred nineteen kilometers per hour while retaining the full six tons of infantry carrying capacity for two platoons. Two front-mounted Small Variable-Speed Pulse Lasers replace the standard machine guns, providing energy-based anti-infantry and anti-light-vehicle weapons that never run out of ammunition.

Heavy ferro-fibrous armor provides seventy-nine points of protection -- the heaviest armor of any APC variant in the entire family -- making the WoB variant exceptionally survivable for a transport vehicle. The fusion engine eliminates the petrochemical fuel dependency of the standard design, granting unlimited operational range. Introduced in 3072, this variant was produced in limited numbers for Word of Blake Militia formations during the Jihad, and its advanced technology makes it both significantly more capable and substantially more expensive than the standard Heavy Wheeled APC.
text.deployment: The Word of Blake variant was produced exclusively for Word of Blake Militia formations during the Jihad, manufactured in limited numbers beginning in 3072. Following the destruction of the Word of Blake, surviving examples were captured by Coalition forces and dispersed across the successor states. The advanced technology incorporated in the design makes maintenance challenging without access to the original production facilities, and the variant has not been reproduced by any post-Jihad manufacturer.

The A configuration replaces the primary variant's heavy large laser with a medium laser and adds two ATM-12 racks in the turret, giving this variant access to the Advanced Tactical Missile system's variable-range engagement capability. Six tons of ATM ammunition feed the launchers, providing adequate but not generous stores for extended operations. This configuration found favor within Alpha Galaxy formations, where its flexible engagement range suited more aggressive tactical doctrines. Several A configurations were captured on Melissia in 3064 during the Jade Falcon offensive, providing the Falcons their first operational experience with ATM weapons in a vehicle mount.

The B configuration entered service in 3068, developed from operational lessons accumulated during the Civil War period and the opening phases of the Jihad. Pod loadout details remain closely held within Wolf in Exile operational records, but the configuration emphasizes adaptability to the varied threat environments encountered during the Blakist conflict. It served primarily with garrison clusters assigned to the defense of Arc-Royal and supporting systems during the extended campaign.

The C configuration appeared mid-Jihad in 3075, developed from sustained operational demands on Clan Wolf in Exile's forces. Built on accumulated combat experience against Word of Blake opponents, this variant incorporates pod loadout adjustments suited to the command and fire-support roles increasingly expected of heavy vehicle assets. The C configuration served as the senior command variant for Heimdall-equipped formations during the later Jihad campaigns, providing force commanders a capable and well-protected mobile platform.

The D configuration entered service in 3092 under the Arc-Royal Defense Cordon, representing the first significant update to the Heimdall's pod loadout since the Jihad era. Incorporating technology advances available through expanded trade and salvage networks, this variant extended the design's operational relevance into the Republic period. It became the standard configuration for Arc-Royal forces through the Dark Age, providing heavy direct-fire support to formations operating without the assault BattleMechs more common in larger House and Clan armies.

The primary configuration is the most widely deployed variant within Clan Wolf in Exile's defensive formations on Arc-Royal and its surrounding systems. The turret mounts a heavy large laser and three Streak SRM-4 launchers, providing reliable combined-arms firepower at most combat ranges. Ammunition stores and supporting heat sinks are positioned within the vehicle body, well protected from battlefield damage. This configuration is the standard assignment for garrison and area-denial missions, where its balanced weapons mix supports both static defense and limited counterattack operations.

The Hephaestus Jump Tank serves exclusively in Clan Hell's Horses formations, deployed in Cavalry Clusters and Strike Clusters. It typically operates alongside artillery-equipped units, using its TAG to call fire missions while its ECM disrupts opposing sensors. The jump capability allows it to rapidly reposition across terrain obstacles that would stop conventional vehicles, giving cluster commanders a fast scout that can keep pace with BattleMech elements in broken terrain. Its high maintenance demands mean that well-supplied units benefit far more from this vehicle than those in the field without technical support.

The anti-infantry variant replaces the standard electronic warfare suite with AP Gauss Rifles for dedicated anti-infantry work. Fielded in units where battle armor or conventional infantry concentrations represent primary threats, this configuration sacrifices the electronic warfare flexibility of the base model for substantially greater effectiveness against soft targets. It retains the jump jets and hover chassis, maintaining the same mobility advantage, and remains capable of direct-fire anti-armor work with its standard armament.

Configuration A converts the Hephaestus into a fire support vehicle, replacing the electronic warfare systems with an Artemis-guided LRM-15 launcher. This configuration operates behind faster screening elements, using its speed to reposition between fire missions. The single ton of ammunition constrains sustained fire, so A-configuration crews conserve their loads for critical missions and rely on resupply to maintain long-duration engagements.

Configuration B is the Hephaestus's most conventional combatant configuration, pairing ER Medium Lasers with a Streak SRM-6 for close-range engagements. The Streak system's lock-on requirement ensures ammunition is never wasted on clear misses. This configuration is used for flank security and close breakthrough screening, often paired with BattleMech elements that need a fast light vehicle to handle opposing scouts and skirmishers.

Configuration C equips the Hephaestus with dual ATM 3 launchers and three tons of ammunition, leveraging the ATM system's ability to fire different munition types for close-range, standard, and extended-range engagements. This configuration is most effective when resupply access allows crews to adjust their ammunition load to mission requirements, making it a flexible all-range option where the standard electronic warfare suite is less critical.

Configuration D, introduced in 3071, addresses the increasing prevalence of battle armor and infantry in opposing forces. AP Gauss Rifles in the turret supplement ER Medium Lasers for anti-armor work, while an ECM Suite and five-ton infantry bay allow the vehicle to continue contributing to combined-arms operations. This configuration is deployed where enemy infantry concentrations are anticipated alongside conventional armor, providing the Horses a single vehicle capable of addressing both threat types.

The Prime configuration serves as the standard electronic warfare variant, fielded across Cavalry Clusters and Strike Clusters. Its combination of TAG and ECM Suite allows it to call indirect artillery fire while disrupting enemy targeting and communication systems. The Prime is typically paired with artillery units or fire support BattleMechs that can exploit its spotting data, and it relies on speed and ECM rather than armor to survive in contested areas.

text.deployment: The standard Hetzer is found throughout the Inner Sphere, concentrated most heavily in militia and planetary defense roles. Its low cost and simple maintenance requirements make it accessible to governments that cannot afford professional combined-arms formations. It is most commonly deployed in pairs or larger groups to compensate for the lack of a turret and limited armor, relying on massed firepower to achieve results that no single vehicle could accomplish alone.

The AC/10 variant arose as supply chains for the heavy Crusher cannon became unreliable during the Succession Wars. Commanders accepted reduced hitting power in exchange for improved sustainability, as AC/10 rounds were more widely available than AC/20 ammunition. It served primarily in the same militia and garrison roles as the standard model, offering a cheaper logistical footprint at the cost of significant firepower reduction.

The most significant redesign in the Hetzer's history, the Cell variant replaces the ICE powerplant with a fuel cell and adopts dual-autocannon armament, distributing firepower across two systems and improving reliability. Produced at Broken Wheel, Indicass, and Layover under the Federated Vilalobos Corporation network, the variant is available to both FVC-affiliated forces and Capellan customers. It retains the Hetzer's low cost and simple maintenance profile while meaningfully improving performance.

Introduced almost simultaneously with the base model, the laser variant substitutes medium lasers for the Crusher cannon. Local commands producing this configuration typically lacked ammunition supply chains but had access to power generation infrastructure. Found throughout the Inner Sphere wherever heat management is acceptable and autocannon rounds are unavailable, it trades the Hetzer's one-shot punch for sustainable energy fire.

Produced exclusively at the Ceres Metals Industries facility on Indicass, the LB-X variant equipped the Capellan Confederation with a version capable of engaging BattleMechs and battle armor at close ranges with cluster munitions. The weapon improved the Hetzer's effectiveness in anti-personnel and light-armor roles. The variant was phased out following the arrival of the Predator Tank Destroyer, which performed the same function more effectively on an improved platform.

A less common field modification, the LRM variant allows the Hetzer to engage at longer ranges, partially compensating for the chassis's inability to rotate its weapon. The vehicle's thin armor still demands concealment or defilade, but the extended engagement range provides more tactical flexibility in placement. Found occasionally across the Inner Sphere wherever long-range missile ammunition supply is reliable.

A Word of Blake Protectorate refit, the Sealed variant adds a C3i computer network and replaces the primary weapon with a Rotary Autocannon inside an NBC-sealed hull, allowing operations in chemically or biologically contaminated environments. The C3i system links the RAC to supporting units, substantially increasing coordinated accuracy. After the Jihad, the design spread through salvage and knowledge transfer, entering small-scale Universal production through the Dark Age.

The SRM variant replaces the primary cannon with short-range missiles, giving the Hetzer a more flexible if shorter-ranged weapons package. Short-range missile ammunition is widely available throughout the Inner Sphere, making this variant viable in supply-constrained environments. It is most commonly found in Capellan Confederation and associated militia forces, where the modification is performed at the unit level.

Developed by Clan Wolf after acquiring the Kalidasa production line, the C variant mounts a Hyper-Assault Gauss rifle in place of the autocannon, extending the basic Hetzer chassis into Clan-technology performance tiers. It provides Clan Wolf warriors an inexpensive long-range fire platform suited to garrison and support roles. The Rasalhague Dominion independently refitted Hetzers on Alshain through Joint Equipment Systems, producing the same Clan-armed configuration for Dominion toumans.

text.overview: The Hi-Scout Drone Carrier is a sixty-ton tracked reconnaissance vehicle produced by ScolTek Associates on Inarcs for the Lyran Commonwealth beginning in 3000. Designed as a mobile command hub for a network of unmanned sensor drones, the Hi-Scout offered planetary garrison forces a cost-effective alternative to committing BattleMechs or manned scout vehicles to forward reconnaissance. The vehicle serves as both the control platform and transport for its complement of six drones, coordinating their movements and processing their sensor data into actionable intelligence for field commanders. Produced initially for the LCAF, the Hi-Scout earned a reputation as one of the most capable dedicated reconnaissance systems of the late Succession Wars era, filling a niche that few other designs attempted to address. ScolTek's facility on Inarcs has maintained continuous production for over eight decades, making the Hi-Scout one of the longest-running vehicle programs in Lyran service.
text.capabilities:
The Hi-Scout's primary strength lies in its StealthMat-Q communications system with MultiTrack coordination, capable of transmitting and monitoring over five hundred channels simultaneously. This allows the vehicle's crew to control six drones, three NapFind hover types and three PathTrak tracked types, carried in a fifteen-ton internal drone hangar. The drones create an overlapping sensor chain that more than doubles the carrier's effective detection range. The vehicle's own sensor suite includes infrared, seismic, audio, motion, radio (including hyperpulse signals), and radar, providing comprehensive coverage within sixty kilometers even without drone support.

Defensively, the Hi-Scout carries only a single SureShot II SRM-2 launcher with one ton of ammunition, reflecting its role as a rear-echelon asset rather than a frontline combatant. Five and a half tons of ArcShield V armor offer limited protection, sufficient to survive encounters with light hovercraft but inadequate against anything heavier. The Vlar 240 internal combustion engine provides a top speed of 64 kilometers per hour, adequate for keeping pace with infantry formations but leaving the vehicle vulnerable if forced to withdraw under fire. The designers clearly prioritized sensor capability and drone coordination over survivability, accepting that the vehicle must rely on friendly forces for protection.
text.deployment: The standard Hi-Scout Drone Carrier serves as the foundation of ScolTek's reconnaissance system. Deployed primarily with LCAF garrison forces and planetary militia commands, the vehicle operates from the rear echelon of defensive positions, directing its drone network to establish sensor coverage across threatened approach corridors. The Hi-Scout's effectiveness depends heavily on terrain and electromagnetic conditions, performing best in open environments with low background radiation where the MultiTrack coordination system can maintain reliable contact with all six drones simultaneously. Garrison commanders typically deploy Hi-Scouts in pairs to provide overlapping coverage and redundancy, with each vehicle responsible for a separate sector of the defensive perimeter.
text.battleHistory:
ScolTek Associates introduced the Hi-Scout Drone Carrier to fill a specific gap in LCAF reconnaissance doctrine. During the late Third Succession War, the technological decline that characterized the era had left most planetary garrisons without reliable surveillance capabilities. Satellite networks were degraded or absent on many worlds, and committing BattleMechs to scouting roles was increasingly untenable given their growing scarcity. The Hi-Scout offered a middle path, deploying expendable drones to gather intelligence while keeping the carrier vehicle and its trained crew safely behind friendly lines.

The system proved its value quickly after entering service, and ScolTek soon found that demand outstripped their production capacity. A broad range of copycat vehicles emerged after the first LCAF Hi-Scouts were captured in a Kurita raid, and scores of ScolTek-produced units were smuggled to other Successor States through various intermediaries posing as mercenary buyers. Within less than twenty years, nearly all five Great Houses possessed Hi-Scout drone networks or effective knock-offs using similar designs. Though the Lyran Intelligence Corps eventually plugged the security breaches that had made this proliferation possible, by 3025 the strategic advantage ScolTek's innovation had originally provided to House Steiner had largely evaporated.

ScolTek maintained steady production on Inarcs throughout the Clan Invasion and Civil War periods. The company's fortunes survived the Jihad intact, suffering no damage from the Word of Blake or other hostile forces, and the factory was operating at full capacity by the end of 3079. The recovery of Star League technology and the development of C3 networking placed the original Hi-Scout design on the table for significant upgrades. ScolTek's engineering staff eventually pursued an ambitious modernization program, producing experimental prototypes that incorporated XL engine technology, enhanced ECM systems, and C3 integration to bring the platform into the modern era.

text.overview:
The Hipparch Cavalry Tank was commissioned in 2562 on the direct orders of First Consul Gregory Amaris of the Rim Worlds Republic, conceived as a fast, aggressive platform to project Republican military power. Designed and built by Diplass Technologies on Apollo, the vehicle was intended to provide the Rim Worlds Army with a capable cavalry asset competitive with Inner Sphere and Star League designs of its day.

Amaris personally championed the program and ordered thousands produced, though critics within the military argued that political considerations rather than battlefield requirements drove the design. The Hipparch's impressive top speed gave Republic cavalry formations genuine offensive potential, but the design's numerous compromises ultimately defined its legacy as much as its battlefield performance.
text.capabilities:
The Hipparch's defining characteristic is its exceptional speed, reaching 151 kph on the hover skirt using the Mercury 140 power plant. This velocity made the vehicle one of the fastest combat platforms of its era, allowing Republican cavalry to conduct high-speed raids, screening operations, and pursuit missions that most opponents could not match.

Armament consists of a pair of Diplass Optimax lasers, one medium and one small, paired with a Harvester SRM 2 missile rack carrying a single ton of reloads. The mix offers reasonable versatility for scout and harassment work, though the payload is modest for a vehicle of its size. Mounting energy weapons on an ICE-powered hull required additional power conversion and heat dissipation equipment, consuming mass that critics argued would have been better spent on armor or firepower.

The resulting protection is thin, only four tons of Forge 9 Flexweave armor distributed with a slight bias toward the front and sides. This proved inadequate against sustained fire from most opponents. Combined with quality control deficiencies from rushed production, the Hipparch's survivability in a stand-up engagement was genuinely poor, requiring crews to rely on speed and maneuver rather than durability.
text.deployment:
The base-model Hipparch served the Rim Worlds Army primarily as a cavalry and scout vehicle during the Reunification War. Its operational profile centered on high-speed reconnaissance, flank screening, and pursuit missions where its velocity offered a decisive advantage. The vehicle's light armament was suited to harassment and anti-infantry duty, though crews frequently improvised field modifications, mounting machine guns for anti-infantry work or trading energy weapons for a larger missile payload.

The most extreme field modification, nicknamed the "Hellhorse" by troops, replaced the entire weapon payload and turret assembly with explosives, converting the vehicle into a crude kamikaze weapon driven into enemy formations or encampments. No factory-built variants were ever produced. With the production line destroyed in 2599, surviving Hipparchs soldiered on until attrition claimed the last of them.
text.battleHistory:
The Hipparch entered service in 2562 as part of First Consul Gregory Amaris's broader effort to modernize the Rim Worlds Army ahead of the Republic's involvement in the Reunification War. Diplass Technologies delivered thousands of vehicles in rapid succession, with production timelines prioritized over quality assurance. Manufacturing defects and field breakdowns accumulated before the design ever reached combat, setting the stage for the problems that would follow.

When Reunification War operations began in 2577, the Hipparch served as the Republic's primary cavalry asset. In reconnaissance and screening roles the vehicle performed reasonably well, using its exceptional speed to cover broad frontages, maintain contact with enemy forces, and conduct slashing attacks through Taurian and Magistracy formations. Star League observers noted the design's effectiveness as a picket and in high-speed offensive operations.

The vehicle's battlefield reputation was nonetheless tarnished by its reliability failures. SLDF analysts estimated that as many as one in ten deaths among Republican Hipparch crews resulted from mechanical malfunction rather than enemy fire, a damning indictment of the rushed production program. Star League technicians who observed the Hipparch's costly performance reportedly concluded the Republic's cavalry needed a more sound design, an assessment that contributed to the subsequent development of the J. Edgar hover tank.

The Hipparch also suffered from misapplication. Despite its light armor, Republican commanders increasingly assigned the vehicle as the anvil in heavy tank maneuvers, using the Hipparch's speed to encircle enemy formations while heavier vehicles delivered the killing blow. The tactic occasionally succeeded but inflicted heavy casualties on the cavalry when enemy armor turned to engage.

Of approximately 7,000 Hipparchs built, fewer than ninety survived the Reunification War. The production line was permanently destroyed in 2599 during the Wbika coup on Apollo, ending replacement production before most surviving vehicles had completed a decade of service.

text.deployment: The standard Hunter remains in production across multiple facilities and is found throughout the Inner Sphere and Periphery. Its broad availability through licensed manufacturers ensures that even the most cash-strapped militias can field effective long-range fire support. Examples of the original Hunter can be found in service with nearly every military that fields tracked combat vehicles.

The most radical departure from the Hunter's design philosophy, the Assault Hunter removes all missile armament in favor of a single Ultra AC/20 with three tons of ammunition. Intended as a short-range ambush platform, the variant proved deeply unpopular with crews accustomed to the Hunter's standoff engagement doctrine. The designation is unofficial, applied by field units rather than Defiance Industries.

The upgraded Hunter entered full production at Defiance Industries in late 3054, incorporating advances recovered from Star League-era technology caches. Twin Coventry Star Fire launchers with Artemis IV fire control doubled the design's missile accuracy. The first new Hunters arrived in Federated Commonwealth units in early 3055, with most deliveries going to Lyran formations. The slower engine and lighter ferro-fibrous armor made the upgraded Hunter more vulnerable than its predecessor, a trade-off that not all crews appreciated.

A common field modification dating to the early Succession Wars, this variant removes the rear-facing flamer in exchange for a third ton of LRM ammunition. Crews who preferred sustained bombardment over any pretense of close-range defense found the trade worthwhile, and the straightforward conversion required no specialized tools or facilities beyond a basic field workshop.

The most recent Hunter variant leverages Clan-specification equipment that became widely available during the Dark Age. A fuel cell engine provides exceptional speed for the weight class, while heavy ferro-fibrous armor offers improved protection. The Defiance-Doombud ClanTech LRM 20 launcher with Artemis IV fire control returns the design to its single-launcher roots with substantially improved accuracy. CASE-protected ammunition bins and a rear-mounted vehicle flamer round out the package.

First appearing in 3059, this variant of the upgraded Hunter replaces one Coventry Star Fire launcher with an extended-range large laser. Additional heat sinks offset the energy weapon's thermal output, and the conversion allows continued missile support alongside direct-fire capability at extended ranges. An extended-range large laser is the favored choice where the equipment is readily available.

Introduced in 3061, this variant swaps one missile launcher for a large pulse laser, pairing accurate energy fire with an expanded ammunition supply for the remaining launcher. The combination of reliable pulse laser accuracy and sustained missile fire makes this one of the more popular upgraded Hunter configurations where equipment is available.

This extensively reworked field variant downgrades the missile launcher to a ten-tube rack and fills the freed tonnage with two forward-mounted medium lasers and paired side-mounted machine guns. The result is a more versatile platform capable of meaningful self-defense at close range, though it sacrifices much of the Hunter's original long-range fire support capability in the process.

Similar in concept to the LRM-10 conversion, this field variant mounts a fifteen-tube launcher with two tons of ammunition and additional close-defense weapons. It retains more of the Hunter's original fire support capability than its smaller-racked sibling while still providing the crew with options against infantry and light vehicles that close to short range.

During the original RWR service period, the Ignis was restricted to elements of the state security apparatus and did not serve with regular military formations. When Stefan Amaris reintroduced the vehicle in 2751, he distributed it through the Amaris Dragoon regiments, ensuring each unit held at least one company of Ignis vehicles and most received in excess of a full battalion. The vehicle's persistent mechanical problems required unusual logistical arrangements. Units typically maintained vehicle pools numbering twice the available crews, ensuring that enough operational vehicles remained available at any given time regardless of how many were down for maintenance or repair.

The SRM configuration arose from recognition that the base Ignis was wholly incapable of engaging any opposition that refused to close to short range. Dropping one flamer from each side and reducing the flamer ammunition by three tons created space for a pair of SRM-2 launchers mounted in the turret, giving crews a meaningful option against light vehicles and BattleMechs. The twin ammunition bins proved highly adaptable, and crews routinely loaded non-standard warheads. Tear gas rounds were used to flush occupants from structures before the remaining flamers were applied. Fragmentation warheads provided antipersonnel coverage in more open areas. Inferno rounds quickly became the preferred loading among experienced Ignis crews, offering the incendiary effect of the vehicle's flamers at a range that kept the Ignis out of immediate return fire.

text.deployment: The standard Indra Infantry Transport serves primarily as an armored personnel carrier in Clan combined-arms Points and Stars, moving infantry between engagements and providing direct-fire support during dismounted operations. Its strong main armament allows it to contribute meaningfully in firefights rather than waiting at a standoff distance while passengers engage, though commanders must account for the vehicle's heat limitations in prolonged close combat. The standard variant serves across multiple Clan toumans with homeworld production spread across the Kerensky Cluster ensuring broad availability. The Quikscell Company facility on Pandora provides an additional production source beginning in the Civil War era, primarily serving Clan Jade Falcon and later Clan Wolf formations in occupation and garrison roles throughout the occupied Inner Sphere.

The (BA) variant was developed in 3069 to address the specialized demands of anti-insurgency and urban pacification operations, particularly in the aftermath of the Hell's Horses invasion of former Lyran worlds. This configuration retains the standard chassis but modifies the infantry bay and loadout to better accommodate battle armor operations and close-range anti-infantry engagements. Production is limited to the Quikscell Company facility on Pandora. The vehicle is issued primarily to Clan Wolf forces operating in occupation zones where anti-insurgency capability takes priority over conventional armored transport. The Indra's association with the Turtle Bay massacre creates a persistent public relations burden for units equipped with this variant, one that Wolf commanders have had limited success in addressing through rebranding or operational distinction.

The Ishtar (Gauss) emerged during the Jihad as Clan Hell's Horses sought to address the standard version's vulnerability against heavier Inner Sphere armor in renewed combat operations. Replacing both autocannons with a Gauss Rifle and a Class 20 Hyper-Assault Gauss Rifle at the cost of the anti-missile system, the variant concentrates its offensive capability into two high-velocity projectile weapons capable of penetrating heavy armor at range. Each weapon carries two tons of ammunition. Field refit kits supported deployment among Hell's Horses formations, supplemented by dedicated factory production at Csesztreg and Kirchbach. The Horses' open sales policy extended availability beyond their own touman, making this variant accessible to outside buyers through the same commercial channels as the standard model.

The Ishtar (Original) served as the first-generation heavy fire support platform across Clan homeworld garrison formations beginning in 2842. Its higher top speed suited offensive operations and rapid redeployment more than the later standard version, but commanders found its lighter armor and reduced weapons load a meaningful liability in sustained engagements. Clan Hell's Horses and Star Adder facilities documented factory lines for this variant, though neither recorded active production during the MUPL surveyed period. By the time the standard Ishtar entered service in 2976, the Original had been largely displaced on garrison rosters, surviving only in mothballed reserve units and training formations where its lighter loadout was considered adequate for low-threat environments.

The standard J-27 is found everywhere in the Inner Sphere and beyond. All Great Houses have manufacturers producing the design, as do the larger Periphery nations. Acme's licensing fees were so low that no manufacturer felt the need to redesign the transport beyond cosmetic changes to nameplates and logos. Among smaller Periphery realms and lawless frontier regions, the J-27 is considered a valuable commodity.

The (Armor) variant adds heavier protection at the expense of some cargo capacity. Introduced during the Succession Wars as a common field modification, it reflects the harsh reality that J-27 crews operating near active combat zones needed more than a half-ton of plating between themselves and enemy fire. The modification is straightforward enough to be performed by any competent vehicle technician.

The (Fusion) variant replaces the standard internal combustion engine with a scavenged fusion powerplant. These tend to be original Star League era vehicles that have survived the ages. The fusion engine frees the vehicle from dependence on fossil fuel supply lines, a significant logistical advantage that makes surviving examples highly prized.

The RISC variant is a Republic Institute of Strategic Combat project launched around 3142. It replaces the standard drivetrain with an 80-rated fuel cell engine and upgraded suspension, while heavy ferro-fibrous armor, a small pulse laser, and a pair of M-Pods provide protection for the transport and its associated viral jammer trailer.

The K-27 'Killjoy' is a Federated Suns combat variant introduced in 2847, designed to look like a typical J-27 while concealing an SRM-4 missile launcher and additional armor. The Federated Suns produces a few dozen each year, intended to make enemies think twice about attacking what appears to be an ordinary ordnance transport.

The Decoy configuration of the RISC trailer supports decoy viral jammer operations, broadcasting false electronic signatures designed to confuse and overwhelm enemy targeting and communications systems. It entered service around 3136 as part of the initial RISC viral jammer deployment program based at the Proving Ground Liberté complex on Terra.

The Homing configuration supports the homing viral jammer variant, which actively tracks and disrupts specific electronic emissions rather than broadcasting general interference. Introduced slightly after the Decoy variant in 3137, it proved especially effective against Clan electronic systems during Operation Mercury and subsequent Republic covert operations across the Inner Sphere.

text.deployment: The standard J. Edgar serves primarily as a fast cavalry and raiding platform. Taurian Defense Force formations used it extensively during the New Vandenburg Revolt, where it proved effective as a core element of light armor formations. Federated Suns commanders concentrate the vehicle in companies attached to elite fast units such as the Avalon Hussars and Deneb Light Cavalry rather than distributing it among general armor formations. The Com Guards also field a limited number drawn from Star League-era stockpiles on Terra.

Developed by Scarborough Manufacturers in 3088, this fuel cell-powered variant was designed to enable production at small automotive repair facilities, reducing dependence on heavy industrial infrastructure in the post-Jihad era. The turret mounts a medium chemical laser and SRM 4, supplemented by two machine guns for anti-infantry coverage. Five and a half tons of heavy ferro-fibrous armor provide solid protection. It is found primarily in Draconis Combine and former Republic of the Sphere formations that adopted the design following Scarborough's production restart in the Dark Age.

This 2793 field modification replaces the SRM 2 racks with a pair of vehicle flamers. It sees use primarily in anti-infantry and defoliant operations where clearing vegetation or fortified positions takes priority over anti-armor work. Found most commonly in secondary garrison forces and militia units that lack regular access to missile resupply, the Flamer variant sacrifices the design's modest anti-armor capability for a role-specialized weapons fit.

text.deployment: The ICE conversion emerged from battlefield necessity in 2854, as field technicians substituted available internal combustion engines for damaged fusion powerplants. The resulting vehicle operates at a reduced flank speed of 129 kilometers per hour and carries one ton less armor than the standard. It is found widely in Periphery garrison forces, planetary militias, and any formation that cannot sustain fusion power systems. The Marian Hegemony's Alphard Trading Company eventually standardized this configuration as a factory production variant.

Produced by Scarborough Manufacturers on Al Na'ir beginning in 3053, this Draconis Combine refit replaces the SRM 2 launchers with two additional medium lasers and a small laser while integrating a C3 slave unit. Six tons of ferro-fibrous armor improve survivability over the standard model. Assigned to Combine C3 networks, the vehicle serves as a fast networked scout that shares targeting data across lance-level formations equipped with C3 master units, multiplying the effectiveness of cooperative fire.

The Marian Hegemony's Alphard Trading Company introduced this updated ICE variant in 3070, replacing the laser and missile armament with a Light Autocannon/5 and four Rocket Launcher 10s. Four and a half tons of heavy ferro-fibrous armor provide improved protection over the earlier ICE model. Designed for Periphery operations where sophisticated power systems are difficult to sustain, the LAC variant serves Marian forces as a light direct fire and anti-infantry platform capable of independent operation far from major supply centers.
